symptom: Cake is sliding or tiers are leaning
causes: Filling too soft or too thick between layers, letting the top tier slip sideways under its own weight.
Layers assembled while still warm, so the frosting hasn't set enough to grip.
No central dowel or support system for a multi-tier stack.
Uneven leveling — a layer sitting on a slight slope tips everything above it.
fixes: Chill each filled layer for at least 20-30 minutes before adding the next.
Use a firmer filling (buttercream or ganache) rather than a very soft one under heavy tiers.
Add a central dowel through multi-tier stacks, not just separator boards.
Re-level every layer with a serrated knife or cake leveler before stacking.

causes: Filling between layers is too soft and is being pushed outward under the weight of the layers above.
The cake wasn't given time to settle before the final crumb coat and finish were applied.
Room temperature is too warm, softening the buttercream after it's already been smoothed.
fixes: Chill the filled, unfrosted cake for at least an hour so the filling firms up before frosting.
Use a firmer filling for tall or heavy layers, saving very soft fillings for shorter builds.
Keep the finished cake somewhere cool until serving, especially in warm weather.

symptom: Cake layers are domed instead of flat
causes: Oven temperature is too high, causing the edges to set before the center finishes rising.
Too much batter for the pan size, forcing it to rise up rather than out.
No insulation around the pan, so the outer edges bake faster than the center.
fixes: Lower the oven temperature slightly and bake a few minutes longer for more even rising.
Fill pans no more than about two-thirds full.
Wrap damp cake strips around the outside of the pan to slow the edges down.
If a dome does form, simply level it off with a serrated knife once cooled.

causes: Not enough gelatin (or it wasn't fully bloomed and dissolved) to stabilize the mixture.
Whipped cream or egg whites were folded in before the base had cooled enough, deflating the aeration.
The mousse wasn't given enough time — or cold enough temperature — in the fridge or freezer to fully set.
fixes: Bloom gelatin fully in cold water and make sure it's completely dissolved into a warm (not hot) base before folding.
Let the flavored base cool to close to room temperature before folding in whipped cream or meringue.
Give mousse at least 4-6 hours in the fridge, or use the freezer for a mousse cake insert.

symptom: Ganache has split or looks greasy
causes: Cream and chocolate were combined at too high a temperature, or too quickly.
The chocolate-to-cream ratio is off for the intended consistency.
The ganache was stirred too vigorously while still very hot, incorporating air and breaking the emulsion.
fixes: Whisk in a splash of warm cream, or warm milk, a little at a time until it comes back together.
For a stubborn split, blend briefly with an immersion blender — this often re-emulsifies it.
Next time, pour warm (not boiling) cream over chopped chocolate and let it sit a minute before stirring gently from the center outward.
